summaries.example: Imagine red-eyed and purple-eyed fruit flies having babies. Each baby gets one chromosome copy from each parent. If purple eyes appear only when a fly gets two purple versions of a gene, babies with one purple version and one red-eye version can still have red eyes. This shows how scientists can track inheritance even before knowing exactly what a gene is made of.
summaries.summary: Molecular genetics can mean three related things: a basic account of how DNA is copied and used, a stronger claim that genes direct nearly all life processes, or a group of laboratory methods for studying and changing DNA. The entry explains how classical genetics first tracked the passing of traits without needing to know the chemical makeup of genes. Molecular research later showed how DNA sequences can be copied and used to make RNA and proteins. Philosophers ask whether this newer knowledge reduces classical genetics to molecular science. Some think different levels of explanation remain useful; others argue that molecular discoveries have joined the older methods into one investigative science. The entry also examines why the word “gene” can be both flexible and helpful, and why claims that genes alone direct development are much stronger than the basic molecular theory.
key_ideas: Classical genetics explained how traits pass from parents to offspring by tracking gene copies.
Molecular genetics added information about DNA copying and how DNA sequences help make RNA and proteins.
A gene can make a difference without being the only cause of a trait. Cells, development, and the environment also matter.
Scientists use genetics not only to explain inheritance but also as a set of tools for investigating living things.
Philosophers disagree about whether molecular genetics replaces classical genetics or works together with it.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand what genetic science can explain—and what it cannot explain by itself. DNA is important, but traits usually depend on many interacting processes inside organisms and on environmental conditions. Learning the difference between a modest scientific claim and a sweeping claim prevents us from treating genes as complete instructions for an entire organism. It also shows how science advances by combining older ways of asking questions with new tools.

important_terms.definition: A molecule that stores genetic material. DNA contains sequences that can be copied and used in cells.
A section of DNA that helps determine a sequence in an RNA or protein molecule in a particular cell situation.
The observable feature of an organism, such as eye color.
The genetic versions an organism carries, including the versions inherited from its parents.
A change or difference in DNA. Some changes can affect a visible trait.
The study of how traits are passed on and how DNA, RNA, and proteins are involved.

questions_to_think_about: Why might scientists keep using a simple inheritance explanation even after learning more molecular details?
Can one small DNA difference have different effects in different environments?
Why might the word “gene” be useful even if scientists cannot always draw one perfect boundary around a gene?

summaries.example: Suppose a DNA change is associated with a different eye color in fruit flies. Classical genetics can explain an inheritance pattern by following the transmission of alternative gene versions and applying the difference principle: in a particular genetic and environmental context, a gene difference can produce a consistent trait difference. Molecular genetics can then investigate how the DNA sequence affects RNA, a protein, or regulation of gene expression. Neither account automatically explains the whole developmental pathway from DNA to eye color.
summaries.summary: The entry presents molecular genetics as a basic theory, a possible fundamental theory, and an investigative practice. Classical genetics explained inheritance by tracking alternative gene versions and relating them to traits, without specifying the physical structure or developmental action of genes. Molecular genetics supplied answers about DNA replication and expression: DNA sequences can be copied, transcribed into RNA, and related in some cases to polypeptide sequences. This success prompted a debate over theoretical reduction. A Nagelian reduction would require suitable connections between the terms and explanatory principles of classical and molecular theories. Some philosophers argue that such connections fail or that molecular detail does not improve explanations of transmission. Others argue that classical genetic differences have been identified molecularly and that molecular research has extended, rather than simply replaced, classical methods. The entry shifts attention toward investigative reasoning, including the use of genetic maps to study DNA. It also distinguishes a modest basic theory from a gene-centered fundamental theory claiming that genes direct organismal development. Developmental and pragmatic approaches challenge that stronger claim while recognizing that genes remain powerful experimental handles.
key_ideas: Classical genetics and molecular genetics are not simply two unrelated sciences: molecular work retools and extends older inheritance methods.
The basic molecular theory explains DNA copying and aspects of expression, but it does not provide general laws connecting every DNA difference to every organismal trait.
The reduction debate concerns epistemological reduction—how theories and explanations relate—not the claim that genes physically cause everything.

Anti-reductionists emphasize that classical concepts and explanations may not connect neatly to molecular descriptions; critics argue that molecular identifications can still preserve classical reasoning.
The gene concept is contested because DNA expression can involve regulatory regions, introns, exons, alternative processing, and products that are RNA rather than proteins.
A unique causal role for genes in determining molecular sequences does not by itself establish the stronger gene-centered theory of organismal development.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction between basic and fundamental theories is important whenever scientific language becomes broader than the evidence supports. Molecular genetics gives strong tools and important explanations concerning DNA, RNA, and proteins. But the entry warns against turning those successes into the claim that genes alone determine whole organisms. The history of genetics also illustrates that scientific progress need not mean that an older level of explanation disappears. Different descriptions can support different experiments and questions.

important_terms.definition: The modest theory that DNA replication and gene expression involve molecular processes connecting DNA sequences with RNA and polypeptide sequences.
A broader claim that genes and DNA direct the development and functioning of organisms as a whole.
The philosophical proposal that one scientific theory is derived from another, lower-level theory through suitable connections and derivations.
An observable trait or characteristic of an organism, whose development can depend on genes, other cellular processes, and environment.
A difference in a gene that produces a corresponding phenotypic difference in a specified genetic and environmental context.
Reasoning used to design experiments, manipulate biological materials, and interpret results, rather than merely derive explanations from laws.
A proposed functional view of a gene as a DNA sequence that determines a particular linear sequence in an expressed product within a cellular context.
The view that biological development depends on interacting processes involving genes, cells, organisms, and environments, rather than genes alone.

questions_to_think_about: Would a more detailed molecular explanation always be a better explanation, or can a higher-level explanation be more useful for a particular question?
What kinds of evidence would be needed to show that a gene concept is coherent despite flexible uses of the term?
How does investigative reasoning differ from deriving one theory from another?
Why might genetic research focus on genes as experimental tools without claiming that genes alone control development?

summaries.example: A class studies two kinds of fruit flies: red-eyed flies and purple-eyed flies. If purple is recessive, a fly needs two purple versions of the relevant gene to show purple eyes. A baby fly receiving a red-eye version from one parent and a purple version from the other may have red eyes. The inheritance rule works even if the class does not yet know the DNA sequence. Later, molecular genetics can investigate how that sequence affects RNA, proteins, or gene regulation.
summaries.summary: Molecular genetics is used in several ways. It can name a basic theory about DNA replication and gene expression, a stronger gene-centered theory about the role of genes in all life processes, or an investigative practice using laboratory techniques to study and alter DNA. The entry begins with classical genetics, which explained how traits are inherited by following gene versions from parents to offspring. This approach did not need to identify the chemical structure of genes or explain development. Molecular biology later explained how DNA can be copied and how DNA sequences can be involved in producing RNA and polypeptides. Philosophers then debated whether classical genetics was being reduced to molecular genetics. One side stresses that classical concepts and explanations do not map neatly onto molecular descriptions. Another argues that molecular discoveries identify the differences used in classical explanations and extend older investigative methods. The entry also discusses uncertainty about a single molecular definition of “gene.” Finally, it separates the well-supported basic theory from the much broader idea that genes alone direct organismal development. Development, regulation, and environmental context make that sweeping idea controversial.
key_ideas: Classical genetics could explain the transmission of traits without explaining what genes were made of or how organisms developed.
Molecular genetics describes DNA as sequences that can be copied and used in making RNA and proteins, while recognizing that expression is more complicated than a simple one-way recipe.
A major philosophical disagreement asks whether molecular genetics reduces classical genetics or whether both kinds of reasoning remain valuable.
Some philosophers emphasize gaps between classical gene concepts and molecular details; others argue that molecular work can preserve the useful difference-making pattern of classical genetics.
The word “gene” has several uses because DNA can include coding regions, regulatory regions, introns, exons, and sequences that help make functional RNA.
The claim that genes are important for making molecular products is weaker than the claim that genes direct all development and functioning.
summaries.why_it_matters: This entry shows why scientific explanations can be more complicated than a simple “everything comes down to DNA” story. Genetics uses several levels of description, and each can help with different questions. Understanding these distinctions helps readers evaluate claims about inheritance, gene function, and development without dismissing either molecular discoveries or the continuing value of classical methods. It also introduces a general philosophical issue: whether deeper explanations always replace broader, more practical ones.

important_terms.definition: The study of inheritance using patterns of traits and gene versions, before needing a molecular description of genes.
A DNA-based account of how genes are copied, expressed, and regulated at the molecular level.
A version of a gene that can differ from another version and contribute to different traits in a given context.
The visible or measurable characteristic produced by an organism, such as eye color.
The set of gene versions an organism has for a particular genetic location or trait.
The process by which information in DNA is used in making RNA and, often, proteins.
The idea that a higher-level scientific theory might be explained or derived using a lower-level theory.
The use of experiments and laboratory methods to discover, test, or manipulate biological processes.

questions_to_think_about: Why can an inheritance explanation be useful even when it leaves out molecular details?
Does learning the physical parts of a process always replace the older way of describing it?
Why might a gene have different boundaries depending on what product or process a scientist is studying?
What is the difference between saying genes help make a protein and saying genes provide the complete plan for an organism?
